COMPLETE EMPIRICAL PLAN  

====================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary strategy: Panel‐data Instrumental Variables (shift–share IV) combined with firm and year (and, in some specifications, country-year) fixed effects.  

Why IV?  
•  Institutional ownership is highly endogenous: managers who expect to improve governance may court institutions; institutions may select firms they already view as improving.  
•  A shift–share (Bartik-type) instrument exploits plausibly exogenous changes in the *supply* of equity capital coming from portfolio rebalancing by the institutions themselves rather than from firm-level fundamentals.  
•  The data set contains the full holdings of each institution, allowing construction of standard “flows-driven” instruments that have become common in finance (e.g., Lewellen 2011; Gormley-Matsa 2014; Crane-Matvos-Potter 2016).  

Mechanics of the instrument  
Step 1:  For every institution j, compute its *external* portfolio-wide shock in year t:  

  FlowShock_{j,t} = (A_{j,t} – A_{j,t-1} × (1+GlobalMktRet_{t})) / A_{j,t-1}  

  where A is total gross assets under management and GlobalMktRet subtracts passive price appreciation.  

Step 2:  Predicted exposure of firm i to flows coming from that institution:  

  PredIO_{i,t} = Σ_{j}  [ w_{i,j,t-1}  ×  FlowShock_{j,t} ]  

  w_{i,j,t-1} is institution j’s % ownership of firm i at t-1.  

Step 3:  Aggregate the above only over the *type* of institutions of interest:  
  • Foreign vs. domestic, or  
  • U.S. vs. non-U.S., or  
  • Common-law vs. civil-law domiciled institutions.  

Intuition: If Japanese retail investors pour money into U.S.-domiciled mutual funds in 2006, the affected funds expand all existing positions roughly proportionally, delivering a positive supply shock to every firm these funds already owned at t-1. That shock is orthogonal to any 2006 governance changes that firm i undertakes.  

Secondary strategy / validity check: Event-study-style difference-in-differences around large *predicted* shocks (e.g., top-quartile PredIO increase vs. bottom quartile) to confirm pre-trends are flat.  

====================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
 IO_{i,t} = fraction of common shares of firm i held at year-end t by *foreign common-law* institutional investors (our headline specification).  

Alternative treatments: total institutional ownership; foreign-all; U.S. only; “independent” vs. “grey” institutions.  

Control group / counterfactual  
 Firms with low or no predicted exposure to foreign common-law flow shocks in the same year *within the same country* serve as the counterfactual; the instrument delivers quasi-random variation in IO within each country-year cell.  

Timing  
 Yearly panel 2003–2008. Governance outcomes are measured at t or t + 1 (to allow for implementation lag).  

No running variable / cutoff is needed (not RDD).  

====================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance (first-stage strength).  
 Fund flow shocks materially move their portfolio weights; prior literature finds F-stats ≫ 10. The broad cross-section and the 2003–2008 “Great Moderation” with large inflows into global funds make this plausible.  

A2. Exclusion / no direct effect.  
 The only channel through which FlowShock_{j,t} affects GOV41_{i,t+1} is via actual ownership IO_{i,t}. Portfolio inflows to a U.S. mutual fund do not change governance of a German firm *unless the fund buys more shares*. Plausible because funds rarely lobby firms they do *not* own.  

A3. Stable unit / no spillovers.  
 One firm’s treatment does not mechanically alter another’s governance, conditional on country-year fixed effects. Given diffuse ownership and >1,500 firms per country, spillovers should be small.  

A4. No differential trends correlated with instrument.  
 Conditional on firm FE and country-year FE, firms with high lagged holdings by, say, U.S. funds should not already be on systematically different governance trajectories. We will test this in an event-study graph.  

A5. Linearity and monotonicity (for LATE interpretation).  
 Higher predicted inflows do not *decrease* actual holdings (no “defiers”), reasonable for long-only institutions.  

====================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Omitted country-level shocks (e.g., local governance reforms) correlated with foreign investor flows.  
 • Include country-year fixed effects.  
 • Instrument is constructed from *foreign* fund flows, so it is orthogonal to domestic policy changes.  

T2. Price-run-up mechanical effect. Rising ownership could be mechanically correlated with stock returns that themselves affect Tobin’s q or CEO turnover (via wealth effects).  
 • Control for annual stock return and lagged market capitalization.  
 • Governance index uses structural attributes that do not mechanically move with price.  
 • Replicate results on governance and on CEO-turnover *sensitivity* subtracting direct price channels.  

T3. Reverse causality in construction of instrument (governance attracts funds whose inflows then enlarge positions further).  
 • Instrument uses *pre-shock* weights w_{i,j,t-1}; any governance change at t cannot influence that.  
 • Event-study confirms parallel pre-trends.  

====================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # high-dimensional FE and IV
library(lmtest)         # Wald tests
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data (assumes csvs are in working directory)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
firm   <- fread("firm_financials.csv")        # Datastream/Worldscope
inst   <- fread("institutional_ownership.csv")# FactSet/LionShares
gov    <- fread("gov_attributes.csv")         # RiskMetrics
ceo    <- fread("ceo_data.csv")               # BoardEx

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct Outcome and Controls
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Governance index (already computed in file)
gov <- gov[, .(firm_id, year, GOV41)]

# Firm-level controls (winsorised at 1/99%)
winsor <- function(x) pmin(pmax(x, quantile(x,0.01,na.rm=TRUE)),
                           quantile(x,0.99,na.rm=TRUE))
firm[, `:=`(
  size  = winsor(log(market_cap)),
  leverage = winsor(total_debt/total_assets),
  mb   = winsor(market_to_book),
  roa  = winsor(roa),
  rdsales = winsor(rnd/sales),
  cash = winsor(cash/assets)
)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Build Shift–Share Instrument
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# (a) Institution-level flow shock
setkey(inst, inst_id, year)
inst[, aum_prev := shift(aum, 1, type="lag"), by = inst_id]
inst[, flow_shock := (aum - aum_prev*(1+global_mkt_ret)) / aum_prev ]

# (b) Lagged firm weights
inst[, weight_lag := shift(holdings_shares, 1, type="lag") /
                       shift(shares_outstanding, 1, type="lag"),
     by = .(inst_id, firm_id)]

# (c) Keep only foreign common-law institutions
inst <- inst[country_inst %in% c("USA","GBR","CAN","AUS") & country_inst != country_firm]

# (d) Predicted ownership for each firm-year
predIO <- inst[!is.na(weight_lag),
               .(pred_io = sum(weight_lag * flow_shock, na.rm=TRUE)),
               by = .(firm_id, year)]

# (e) Actual ownership (treatment)
actualIO <- inst[, .(io = sum(holdings_shares / shares_outstanding, na.rm=TRUE)),
                 by = .(firm_id, year)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Merge everything
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("firm_id","year"), all=TRUE),
             list(firm, gov, predIO, actualIO))
dt <- na.omit(dt)   # keep balanced observations

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Main IV specification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_spec <- feols(GOV41 ~ io + size + leverage + mb + roa + rdsales + cash |
                        pred_io | firm_id + year,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~ country)

summary(iv_spec)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: Add country-year FE & event-study
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_ctyyr <- feols(GOV41 ~ io + size + leverage + mb + roa |
                          pred_io | firm_id + country^year,
                  data = dt, cluster = ~ country)
summary(iv_ctyyr)

# Event-study (pre-trends) for treated vs. control
dt[, quartile := cut(pred_io, quantile(pred_io, probs=seq(0,1,0.25)),
                     labels=FALSE, include.lowest=TRUE), by=year]
event <- feols(GOV41 ~ i(rel_year, quartile==4, ref=-1) | firm_id + year,
               data = make_event_panel(dt, shock_year="year", id="firm_id",
                                       treat_var = (quartile==4)), cluster=~country)
iplot(event)
```

====================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic prior: A 10 percentage-point increase in foreign common-law institutional ownership should raise the GOV41 index by roughly 0.15–0.25 standard deviations (≈ 1–1.5 attributes), increase the performance-sensitivity of CEO turnover by 3–5 p.p., and raise Tobin’s q by ~0.05–0.08. The effect should be strongest in civil-law countries where baseline governance is weakest.  

====================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1. Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10): 1  
C2. Instrument exogeneity / exclusion plausibility: 0.5  
C3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): 0.8  
C4. Parallel pre-trends / no differential trend (event study): 0.8  
C5. Robustness across alternative specifications (country–year FE, placebo years): 0.9  

Overall: 4.0 / 5 (reasonably credible with remaining concern over exclusion).
